objective: By the end of this lesson you can name each class and type of airspace, find it on a sectional chart, and state the weather, radio, equipment and pilot rules for flying VFR in it, including special VFR, special use airspace, TFRs and SFRAs.
why: Most airspace violations happen because a pilot did not know where the lines were or what they required. Knowing the airspace keeps you legal, keeps you away from traffic and hazards, and protects your certificate.

prereading.what: All of Chapter 15. Study Figures 15-1, 15-8 and 15-9 closely.

warmup: You are cruising at 2,500 feet AGL on a hazy day, 2 miles below a cloud deck. Can you tell, from your chart alone, whether that is legal VFR right where you are?

key_terms.def: Class A, B, C, D and E. ATC service is provided according to the class. VFR pilots still see and avoid.
Class G. ATC has no authority to control traffic, but VFR weather minimums still apply.
The minimum flight visibility and distance from clouds for VFR flight in each class and altitude (14 CFR 91.155).
An ATC clearance to fly VFR in a surface area below basic VFR minimums: clear of clouds, at least 1 SM visibility (14 CFR 91.157).
Airspace where certain activities must be confined or where limits are placed on other aircraft: prohibited, restricted, warning, MOA, alert, CFA.
Temporary flight restriction. Issued by FDC NOTAM. Check it before every flight.
Special Flight Rules Area / Special Air Traffic Rules. Areas listed in 14 CFR part 93 with their own extra rules (for example, the Washington DC SFRA).
Airspace within 30 NM of the primary airports listed in Part 91 Appendix D, surface to 10,000 feet MSL, where an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out are required.
The fuzzy shaded band on a sectional. Magenta = Class E starts at 700 feet AGL. Blue = Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL (abutting Class G).

chunks.title: The big picture: categories, types and classes

body.p: Airspace has two categories: regulatory and nonregulatory. Inside those are four types: controlled, uncontrolled, special use, and other airspace [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].

bullets: Regulatory: Class A, B, C, D and E, plus restricted and prohibited areas [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].
Nonregulatory: MOAs, warning areas, alert areas, controlled firing areas and national security areas [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].
Controlled airspace = Class A, B, C, D and E [[1:377|PHAK 15-2]].
Uncontrolled airspace = Class G, everything not designated A, B, C, D or E [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].

body.p: The classes are legally designated in 14 CFR part 71. The actual list of Class A to E areas is in FAA Order JO 7400.11M, made part of the rule by reference [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]].

callout.text: When two airspace designations overlap, the rules of the more restrictive one apply. A is most restrictive, then B, C, D, E, and G is least [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]] [[33:175|AIM 3-1-3]].

check.q: Is a restricted area regulatory or nonregulatory airspace?
check.a: Regulatory. Restricted and prohibited areas are regulatory; MOAs, warning, alert, CFA and NSA are nonregulatory [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].

body.p: Class A is generally 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600, including waters within 12 NM of the coast of the 48 contiguous states and Alaska [[1:377|PHAK 15-2]]. All flight there is IFR, under an ATC clearance received before entering [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]]. Class A is not shown on VFR charts [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]].
Class B is generally surface to 10,000 feet MSL around the busiest airports. It is built in layers, like an upside-down wedding cake [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]].

bullets: Entry: you need an ATC clearance before entering, no matter the weather [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131]]. Listen for the words "cleared into the Class Bravo."

Pilot: at least a private pilot certificate, or a student who meets 61.94 or 61.95 [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(b)]]. Some primary airports need at least a private certificate to take off or land [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]].
Equipment: two-way radio, operating transponder with altitude reporting, and ADS-B Out [[60:456|14 CFR 91.131(c),(d)]].
Weather: 3 SM visibility, clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].
Service: VFR aircraft get sequencing and separation inside Class B [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]].

callout.text: Stay well clear of Class B edges, mainly where the floor is 3,000 feet AGL or less or near a VFR cruising altitude [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]]. Speed under a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor: no more than 200 knots [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(c)]].

check.q: Approach says "Cessna 123, radar contact." Can you enter Class B?
check.a: No. Class B needs a clearance. Radar contact is not a clearance [[33:179|AIM 3-2-3]] [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]].

body.p: Class C: usually surface to 4,000 feet above airport elevation (charted in MSL). It has a 5 NM core from the surface and a 10 NM shelf from no lower than 1,200 feet up to 4,000 feet above the airport [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]]. There is a procedural outer area, normally 20 NM, that is not charted [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].
Class D: usually surface to 2,500 feet above airport elevation (charted in MSL), around an airport with an operating control tower [[33:185|AIM 3-2-5]].

head: Class C
Class D
rows: Two-way radio contact before entering [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]]
Two-way radio contact before entering [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)]]
Two-way radio, altitude-reporting transponder, ADS-B Out [[60:455|14 CFR 91.130(d)]]
200 kt max at/below 2,500 AGL within 4 NM of primary airport [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]

callout.text: "Standby" rule: If ATC answers with YOUR call sign ("Cessna 123, standby"), radio contact is established and you may enter Class C or D. If ATC answers without your call sign ("Aircraft calling, standby") or says "remain outside," you may NOT enter [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

body.p: Departing a satellite airport with no tower inside C or D: call the controlling ATC facility as soon as practicable after takeoff [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(2)]]. Part-time towers: when the tower closes, Class D becomes Class E or Class G. The Chart Supplement tells you which [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

Radio failure in Class D under VFR: you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you get a clearance to land (light signals) [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)]].

check.q: Your Class D destination tower closes at 2100 local. What class is the surface area after that, and where do you find out?
check.a: It reverts to Class E or Class G. The Chart Supplement airport listing says "other times Class E" or "other times Class G" [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

body.p: Class E is controlled airspace that is not A, B, C or D. A large amount of U.S. airspace is Class E [[1:377|PHAK 15-2]].

bullets: Most areas: Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL. Many others: at the surface or at 700 feet AGL [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].
Where a chart shows no Class E base, Class E starts at 14,500 feet MSL [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].
Class E goes up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL. All airspace above FL 600 is also Class E [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].
Federal airways (V-routes) are Class E from 1,200 feet AGL to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL unless otherwise specified [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].
Class E surface areas need weather reporting at the airport [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].

body.p: Class G goes from the surface up to the base of the overlying Class E [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]]. No ATC control, but VFR minimums still apply.
At a nontowered airport in Class G (and Class E): make all turns to the left unless the airport shows light signals or markings for right turns [[60:451|14 CFR 91.126(b)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127]].

callout.text: Towered airport in Class G or E (no Class D): you must still talk to the tower. Make contact before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]].
An aircraft flying exactly at the base of a Class E area counts as being in the airspace below it [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]].

check.q: No Class E base is charted where you are flying. Where does Class E begin?

chunks.title: Transponder and ADS-B Out: where you need them

body.p: An operating transponder with Mode C altitude reporting is required in these places (unless ATC authorizes otherwise) [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]]:

bullets: Class A, B and C airspace.
Within 30 NM of the Appendix D, section 1 airports (the Mode C veil), surface to 10,000 feet MSL.
Above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class B or C, up to 10,000 feet MSL.
At and above 10,000 feet MSL over the 48 states and DC, excluding at and below 2,500 feet AGL.
Within 10 NM of the Appendix D, section 2 airports, surface to 10,000 feet MSL (except below 1,200 feet outside that airport's surface area).

body.p: ADS-B Out is required in almost the same airspace: Class B and C, the 30 NM veil, above B and C up to 10,000 feet MSL, and Class E at and above 10,000 feet MSL excluding at and below 2,500 feet AGL. It also adds Class E at and above 3,000 feet MSL over the Gulf within 12 NM of the coast [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]].
In all controlled airspace, if your transponder works, keep it on, including Mode C [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. If you have ADS-B Out, keep it transmitting at all times [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(f)]].

callout.text: Inoperative transponder or ADS-B Out: you can ask ATC at any time to fly to your destination or a repair shop. No transponder or ADS-B Out installed: request at least 1 hour before the flight [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)]] [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]].

check.q: You will overfly a Class C at 6,500 feet MSL. Its ceiling is 4,000 feet above the airport. Do you need Mode C and ADS-B Out?
check.a: Yes. Both are required above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]].

body.p: You may not fly VFR when flight visibility or distance from clouds is less than the table below for your class and altitude [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. This table is for airplanes (helicopter rows left out).

callout.text: "3-152": in C, D and E below 10,000 MSL it is 3 SM and 1,000 above, 500 below, 2,000 horizontal. "5-111" at or above 10,000 MSL (E, and G above 1,200 AGL): 5 SM and 1,000 above, 1,000 below, 1 SM horizontal. Class B is the odd one: 3 SM and clear of clouds.

body.p: Three more rules near airports:

bullets: Night, Class G below 1,200 AGL: an airplane may fly clear of clouds with at least 1 SM visibility if it is in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].
Surface area of controlled airspace: no VFR beneath the ceiling when the ceiling is less than 1,000 feet (unless special VFR) [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]].

Surface area of Class B, C, D or E: to take off, land or enter the pattern VFR, ground visibility must be at least 3 SM (flight visibility 3 SM if ground visibility is not reported) [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].

callout.text: Student pilots have stricter limits: no PIC with flight or surface visibility below 3 SM by day or 5 SM at night, or without visual reference to the surface [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6),(7)]] [[33:176|AIM 3-1-4]].

check.q: Class E at 9,500 feet MSL. What visibility and cloud clearance do you need? What changes at 10,500 feet MSL?
check.a: At 9,500: 3 SM, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal. At 10,500: 5 SM, 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

body.p: Special VFR lets you fly in a surface area when the weather is below basic VFR. It is allowed only below 10,000 feet MSL, inside the upward extension of the lateral limits of the controlled airspace designated to the surface for an airport [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(a)]].

bullets: You need an ATC clearance [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(1)]].
Stay clear of clouds [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(2)]].
Flight visibility at least 1 SM (airplanes) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(3)]].
Between sunrise and sunset only, unless you are instrument rated and current and the airplane is IFR-equipped [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]].
To take off or land: ground visibility at least 1 SM, or flight visibility 1 SM if ground visibility is not reported [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]].

body.p: Ask the tower if there is one. In a Class E surface area, ask the nearest tower, FSS or center [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. The clearance has no specific altitude, because you must stay clear of clouds. You are still responsible for obstacle and terrain clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

callout.text: Fixed-wing special VFR is prohibited at some Class B and C airports (Part 91 Appendix D, section 3). These are marked "NO SVFR" above the airport name on the chart [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]. The SVFR clearance ends when you leave the surface area [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

check.q: You are a private pilot without an instrument rating. Can you get special VFR out of a Class D airport at night?
check.a: No. Airplane SVFR at night needs an instrument-qualified pilot and an IFR-equipped airplane [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

chunks.title: Reading airspace on the sectional chart

bullets: Class B: solid blue lines. Ceiling over floor in solid blue numbers, last two zeros dropped (80 over 40 = 8,000 to 4,000 MSL). A + before a floor means "above" that altitude; at or below it you are outside Class B [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].
Class C: solid magenta lines. Same ceiling/floor style. "T" ceiling = up to but not including the Class B floor above. "SFC" = surface [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].
Class D: blue dashed line. Ceiling in a box. A minus sign means "surface up to but not including" that altitude [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].
Class E surface area: magenta dashed line [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].
Class E starting at 700 feet AGL: magenta vignette. Floors other than 700 feet next to Class G (normally 1,200 AGL): blue vignette [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]] [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].
Mode C 30 NM veil: solid magenta circle labeled "MODE C & ADS-B OUT 30 NM" [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].
Class A is not drawn on VFR charts [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

callout.text: Magenta boxes near a Class C give the approach frequency to call before you enter, generally within 20 NM [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].
Airports under Part 93 rules have their name boxed on the chart [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

check.q: A Class C sector is labeled T over 25. What does it mean?
check.a: Floor 2,500 feet MSL; ceiling up to but not including the floor of the overlying Class B [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

head: Type
Chart label
What it means for a VFR pilot
rows: Flight is prohibited. Security or national welfare [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]].
Unusual, often invisible hazards (artillery, missiles). Do not enter when active without permission of the using or controlling agency [[1:378|PHAK 15-3]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133]].
Hazardous activity, from 3 NM outward from the coast. U.S. does not have sole jurisdiction [[1:379|PHAK 15-4]].
Military training. VFR may enter but use extreme caution. Contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories before entering an active MOA [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].
High volume of pilot training or unusual activity. Everyone is equally responsible for collision avoidance [[1:379|PHAK 15-4]].
Activity stops when an aircraft approaches. No need to change your path [[33:191|AIM 3-4-7]].

body.p: Chart colors: prohibited, restricted and warning areas are drawn with blue hatched borders; MOAs and alert areas with magenta hatched borders [[2:45|Chart Users' Guide p.45]].

Hours, altitudes and the controlling agency are listed on the chart [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1]]. You can ask the using or controlling agency for status; their frequency is in the chart margins [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]]. For MOA status, call any FSS within 100 miles [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]]. Temporary MOAs and temporary restricted areas are not charted; check NOTAMs [[33:191|AIM 3-4-3, 3-4-5]].
National security areas: pilots are asked to avoid them voluntarily. Flight may be temporarily prohibited by NOTAM [[33:192|AIM 3-4-8]].

check.q: Is it legal to fly VFR through an active MOA?
check.a: Yes, but use extreme caution and contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories first [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

body.p: A TFR is issued by FDC NOTAM. It starts with "FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS," then gives the location, effective time, area in statute miles, altitudes, the FAA coordination facility and phone, and the reason [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]] [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]].
Common reasons [[33:195|AIM 3-5-3]]:

bullets: Hazards on the surface, disaster relief aircraft, or sightseeing crowds over an incident [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137]].
The President, Vice President or other public figures [[60:459|14 CFR 91.141]].
Space flight operations [[60:459|14 CFR 91.143]].
Air shows and major sporting events [[60:460|14 CFR 91.145]].

body.p: Disaster/hazard TFRs are normally limited to within 2,000 feet above the surface and a 3 NM radius [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]]. Always read the actual NOTAM; sizes vary.

callout.text: It is the pilot's job to know about TFRs on the route. TFR incursions have led to security investigations and certificate suspensions [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]]. Only TFRs related to national security are charted [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

check.q: Where must you look to learn about a TFR for a VIP visit tomorrow?
check.a: In the NOTAMs (FDC NOTAM) during preflight. Such TFRs are not on the sectional [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]] [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

chunks.title: SFRAs, SATRs and other airspace areas

body.p: Part 93 sets special air traffic rules (SATR) for certain areas. Some are designated Special Flight Rules Areas (SFRAs). If you fly to, from or within one, you must follow its Part 93 rules unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:202|AIM 3-5-7]]. SFRAs are shown on sectional, terminal area and helicopter charts [[33:202|AIM 3-5-7]].

Washington DC SFRA: surface to, but not including, FL 180, within 30 miles of the DCA VOR/DME. It contains the DC Flight Restricted Zone (FRZ) [[60:705|14 CFR 93.335]]. To fly VFR in the SFRA you must [[60:705|14 CFR 93.339]]:

bullets: Have a working two-way radio and talk to ATC before entering and the whole time inside.
Have a working altitude-reporting transponder and squawk a discrete code from ATC. Code 1200 is not allowed [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].
File and activate a DC SFRA or FRZ flight plan.
Get a Class B clearance before entering the Class B, and follow Class D rules in Class D.
Complete the FAA Special Awareness Training to fly VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].

callout.text: DC SFRA/FRZ is national defense airspace. Even an accidental violation can bring civil penalties and certificate action. Knowing or willful violations can bring criminal prosecution [[60:704|14 CFR 93.333]].

body.p: Other airspace areas to know:

bullets: Military training routes: usually below 10,000 feet MSL at more than 250 knots. Four digits (VR1207) = no segment above 1,500 AGL; three digits (IR206) = some segment above 1,500 AGL [[33:193|AIM 3-5-2]] [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2]].
VFR flyway: general path to avoid Class B. No clearance needed [[33:198|AIM 3-5-5]].
VFR corridor: a "hole" through Class B. No clearance needed [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].
VFR transition route: a specific route through Class B, C or D. Talk to ATC; a clearance is still required for Class B [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].
TRSA: extra radar service. VFR participation is voluntary but encouraged [[1:382|PHAK 15-7]].
Parachute jump sites: listed in the Chart Supplement; frequently used ones are on the sectional [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]].

check.q: You are inside the DC SFRA with ATC's code but you set 1200 by habit after a frequency change. Problem?
check.a: Yes. You must transmit the assigned discrete code; 1200 is not allowed in the DC SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].

body.p: Airspace risk comes from not knowing where you are, not knowing what the airspace needs, or not having what it needs (radio contact, clearance, equipment, weather). It grows with haze, workload, and unfamiliar areas.

bullets: Before flight: check NOTAMs for TFRs and SUA activation [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]] [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]]. Read the chart along the whole route, including the floors above you.
Plan altitudes that keep you clear of Class B floors with a margin, especially where the floor is 3,000 feet AGL or less [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]]. Use VFR flyway planning charts [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]].
Know your exits: where you can turn away or descend before a boundary.
Call early. Start contact far enough out that you will not enter Class C or D before two-way communication is established [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].
Flight following does not relieve you of clearance or communication duties for Class B, C or D [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].
If weather drops below minimums for your airspace, do not push. Turn around, divert, or (if eligible and in a surface area) request special VFR.

callout.text: Inside Class B or C, ATC service does not relieve you of see-and-avoid, terrain clearance or VFR weather minimums. If an ATC heading or altitude would put you in a cloud, tell ATC and get a new instruction [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:184|AIM 3-2-4]].

check.q: You are getting flight following from approach and drifting toward a Class D. Must you still call the tower?
check.a: Yes. The pilot is responsible for meeting the radio and clearance requirements for B, C and D even when receiving radar advisories [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: ceilings, floors, vignettes and special areas

body.p: Controlled airspace on a sectional is drawn with lines, numbers and color bands. Learn the numbers first. For Class C the top number is the ceiling and the bottom number is the floor, in hundreds of feet MSL. So 48 over 30 means 3,000 ft up to 4,800 ft MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

Class D shows one number in a dashed box, also in hundreds of feet MSL. A minus sign in front, as in -27, means from the surface up to but not including 2,700 ft MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]] [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

A magenta dashed line is Class E that starts at the surface. Where Class E starts above the ground, a soft color band called a vignette shows it. Magenta means a floor of 700 ft AGL. Blue means a floor higher than 700 ft, usually 1,200 ft AGL, next to Class G. Class E exists at 1,200 ft AGL unless the chart shows another floor [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]] [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

Some areas are not Class A to E. A broken magenta line marks a National Security Area. A broken blue line marks a TFR relating to national security. An ADIZ has its own dotted symbol [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

callout.text: The chart shows only the TFRs that relate to national security. Most TFRs are not charted, so check NOTAMs before every flight [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

Class E shows a magenta dashed outline, a magenta vignette band for 700 feet AGL, a second magenta band marked Class G, and a blue band for 1,200 feet AGL.

f9.caption: Chart Users' Guide: national security areas, SFRAs, TFRs, ADIZ and TRSAs.
f9.alt: Text with small symbols. A broken magenta line marks a National Security Area, a blue-and-white bar marks an SFRA, a screened blue bar marks the Washington DC FRZ, a broken blue line marks TFRs relating to national security, a dotted magenta band marks an ADIZ, red cross-hatching marks a National Defense Airspace TFR and a gray bar marks a TRSA.

scenario.title: Saturday trip to the lake
scenario.setup: You are a new private pilot in a C172 with a transponder and ADS-B Out. You plan a 70 NM VFR flight from a nontowered field under a Class B shelf with a 3,000 feet MSL floor to a towered Class D airport near a lake. The route passes near a MOA, and the forecast says haze with visibility 4 to 5 SM. The destination METAR at takeoff time reads: ceiling 900 broken, visibility 4 SM.

questions.q: What must you check before engine start that is not printed on the sectional?
questions.a: NOTAMs for TFRs on the route [[1:381|PHAK 15-6]], SUA activation by NOTAM [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]], MOA status (temporary MOAs are not charted) [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]], and whether the Class D tower is open (Chart Supplement) [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

questions.q: Under the Class B shelf, you planned 3,500 feet MSL because the course is eastbound. What is wrong, and what should you do?
questions.a: 3,500 MSL is inside Class B (floor 3,000 MSL) without a clearance [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]]. VFR cruising altitudes apply only more than 3,000 feet above the surface anyway [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]]. Fly lower with a margin below the floor, or get a Class B clearance. AIM warns about flying near floors of 3,000 feet AGL or less [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]].

questions.q: The MOA is active. Can you fly through it?
questions.a: Legally yes, but with extreme caution. Contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories before entering, or route around [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

questions.q: With a 900-foot ceiling at the Class D, can you land under basic VFR?
questions.a: No. In a surface area you may not fly VFR beneath a ceiling of less than 1,000 feet [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. You would need a special VFR clearance: clear of clouds, at least 1 SM, daytime for a non-instrument pilot [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157]]. A wise new pilot with low experience in haze would divert or delay instead.

questions.q: You call the tower 10 NM out and hear "Aircraft calling Lake Tower, standby." May you enter the Class D?
questions.a: No. ATC did not use your call sign, so two-way communication is not established. Stay outside until they call you by call sign [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

skills.do: State the basic VFR weather minimums for each class and altitude, and decide from a METAR/forecast whether a planned flight (including takeoff and landing in a surface area) can be done legally VFR.
skills.practice: Write the 91.155 table from memory until perfect. Then take real METARs for airports on a practice route and decide: legal VFR, special VFR needed, or no-go [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c),(d)]].

skills.do: Point to each airspace on a sectional along your cross-country route, give its floor and ceiling, and say what radio contact, clearance and equipment (transponder, ADS-B Out) you need there.
skills.practice: On a current sectional, trace your planned route and label every boundary you cross or fly under. For each, say the entry rule (clearance for B, two-way radio for C/D) and equipment [[1:384|PHAK 15-9]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215]].

skills.do: Identify SUA on the route and explain how to check its status; find any TFRs; and if near a Part 93 area or SFRA, state its rules and how you will comply or avoid it.
skills.practice: During preflight, pull the NOTAMs for your route and find any TFRs. Look up the controlling agency for each MOA or restricted area in the chart margin [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]]. If near DC, complete the Special Awareness Training [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].

quiz.q: What are the basic VFR weather minimums in Class D airspace?
options: 5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
1 SM; clear of clouds
3 SM; clear of clouds
3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
quiz.why: Class C, D and E below 10,000 MSL all use 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000 [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

quiz.q: What are the VFR minimums in Class B?
options: 1 SM and clear of clouds
3 SM and clear of clouds
3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
5 SM and clear of clouds
quiz.why: Class B is 3 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

quiz.q: Daytime, Class G, 1,000 feet AGL. What is the minimum flight visibility for an airplane?
options: 1 SM
1/2 SM
3 SM
5 SM
quiz.why: Class G at 1,200 AGL or less by day: 1 SM and clear of clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]].

quiz.q: Before entering Class C airspace, a VFR pilot must:
options: Receive an ATC clearance
File a flight plan
Establish two-way radio communication with the ATC facility
Hold at least a private pilot certificate
quiz.why: Class C requires two-way radio contact before entry; no clearance or certificate level required [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

quiz.q: Which is required for special VFR in an airplane?
options: An ATC clearance, 3 SM flight visibility, and 500 feet below the clouds
An ATC clearance and ground visibility of at least 3 SM, reported by the tower
An instrument rating at all times, and an instrument-equipped airplane
An ATC clearance, clear of clouds, and at least 1 SM flight visibility
quiz.why: SVFR: ATC clearance, clear of clouds, 1 SM flight visibility; instrument qualifications only needed at night [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157]].

quiz.q: A magenta vignette on a sectional chart means:
options: Class E begins at 1,200 feet AGL
Class D boundary
Class E begins at 700 feet AGL
Mode C veil
quiz.why: Magenta vignette = controlled airspace floor at 700 feet AGL; blue vignette = other floors (normally 1,200 AGL) next to Class G [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

quiz.q: Within the 30 NM Mode C veil, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, you need:
options: Only a two-way radio and a current ATC clearance for each leg
An ATC clearance and an instrument-equipped airplane for each leg
An instrument rating, plus a current IFR-approved GPS in the airplane
An altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out
quiz.why: Required within 30 NM of Appendix D, section 1 airports [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(2)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(2)]].

quiz.q: You call approach and hear "Aircraft calling Springfield Approach, standby." May you enter the Class C?
options: Yes, "standby" means contact is made
Yes, if your transponder is on
No, ATC did not use your call sign
Only if below 2,500 AGL
quiz.why: Without your call sign, two-way communication is not established [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

quiz.q: What may a VFR pilot do with a restricted area that is active?
options: Fly through it if you stay above 1,500 feet AGL
Enter freely, since a restricted area is advisory only
Enter only with permission of the using or controlling agency
Enter if you are talking to any flight service station
quiz.why: No flight in a restricted area contrary to its restrictions without permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133]].

quiz.q: Which transponder code is NOT allowed while flying VFR in the Washington DC SFRA?
options: 1234 in a towered SFRA pattern
A discrete code from ATC
Any code assigned by Potomac Approach
quiz.why: No pilot may use code 1200 in the DC SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].

quiz.q: A Class C sector on the chart is marked 48 over 30. What are its limits?
options: 4,800 ft up to 3,000 ft AGL
300 ft up to 480 ft MSL
3,000 ft up to 4,800 ft MSL
30 ft up to 48 ft AGL
quiz.why: The numbers are in hundreds of feet MSL. The top is the ceiling and the bottom is the floor [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

quiz.q: A Class D area is marked with a boxed -27. What does the minus sign mean?
options: Class D is active only during night hours
Class D starts at 2,700 feet MSL and goes up from there
The Class D ceiling is 2,700 ft above ground level
From the surface up to but not including 2,700 ft MSL
quiz.why: A minus sign before the figure means from the surface to, but not including, that altitude. The figure is in hundreds of feet MSL [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]] [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p 16]].

quiz.q: What does the blue vignette band on the legend show?
options: Class E floor of 1,200 ft AGL next to Class G
Class E that begins right at the surface
Class E with a floor of 700 ft AGL above ground
A Class D area around a towered airport
quiz.why: A blue vignette marks controlled airspace with a floor other than 700 ft that laterally abuts Class G. A magenta vignette marks a 700 ft AGL floor [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]].

quiz.q: On the national security legend, what does a broken blue line mark?
options: A TFR relating to national security
A Terminal Radar Service Area
An Air Defense Identification Zone
A National Security Area
quiz.why: A broken blue line marks TFR areas relating to national security. A broken magenta line marks a National Security Area [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

quiz.q: You plan to fly VFR through Class B airspace at 4,000 ft MSL. What does 14 CFR 91.131(a)(1) require before you operate in that area?
options: Two-way radio contact with the facility alone
A filed IFR flight plan for the whole trip
Only a transponder code of 1200 on the panel
An ATC clearance from the controlling facility
quiz.why: In Class B the operator must receive an ATC clearance before operating in the area [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]]. Radio contact alone is the Class C and D rule.

takeaways: Class B needs a clearance; Class C and D need two-way radio contact before entry.
Memorize the 91.155 table: 3-152 for C, D and E below 10,000 MSL; Class B is 3 SM clear of clouds.
No VFR under a ceiling below 1,000 feet in a surface area; special VFR needs a clearance, clear of clouds and 1 SM.
Mode C and ADS-B Out: Class A, B, C, the 30 NM veil, above B and C to 10,000 MSL, and at/above 10,000 MSL (not within 2,500 AGL).
Check NOTAMs for TFRs and SUA every flight; TFR incursions can cost you your certificate.
Part 93 SFRAs like DC have their own rules: radio, discrete code, flight plan, and training.
cfi_notes: Students mix up the Class G night rows: below 1,200 AGL at night it is 3 SM and 500/1,000/2,000, with the 1 SM clear-of-clouds pattern exception within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].
Have students read real sectional altitudes aloud (80/40, T/25, boxed -27). Examiners like the T ceiling and the minus sign.
Common error: thinking flight following means they are cleared into Class B, or that "standby" without a call sign permits Class C/D entry.
Examiners often ask where Mode C/ADS-B Out is needed above Class C and above 10,000 MSL; have students explain the 2,500 AGL exclusion.
Walk the student through a part-time Class D: what the airspace becomes when the tower closes and where to confirm it in the Chart Supplement.
Tie student pilot limits (3 SM day / 5 SM night) to this lesson so solo students know their legal minimums are stricter than 91.155 [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89]].
Use the flight school's local sectional for the S2 drill; the lesson figures are legend examples only.
gaps: Standard dimensions of sporting-event and VIP TFRs (published in FDC NOTAMs) are not in these resources; students must read each NOTAM.
Detailed rules for Part 93 areas other than the DC SFRA (for example Los Angeles or Grand Canyon SFRAs) are only referenced, not taught here.
A current local sectional chart and Chart Supplement are needed for the S2 chart-reading drill; they are not among the uploaded resources.
The 61.94/61.95 student pilot Class B training and endorsement details are only mentioned (covered in the pilot qualifications lesson).

activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: You need an ATC clearance to enter
A student pilot needs special training and an endorsement to fly solo here

A 5 NM core and a 10 NM shelf
Usually surface to 4,000 feet above the airport
An uncharted outer area, normally 20 NM
Usually surface to 2,500 feet above the airport
ATC gives VFR aircraft no separation service

activities.title: Match the airspace to its VFR minimums
activities.intro: Tap an airspace, then the visibility and cloud clearance it needs.

pairs.l: Class E at or above 10,000 MSL
Class G day, 1,200 AGL or less
Class G day, above 1,200 AGL, below 10,000 MSL

activities.title: Read the sectional
activities.intro: Tap a chart symbol, then what it tells you.

pairs.r: Part 93 special air traffic rules apply
Fixed-wing special VFR is not allowed there

cards.s: You may fly VFR through an active MOA.
cards.why: Yes. It is legal, but use extreme caution and call the controlling agency for traffic advisories before you enter [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

cards.s: In an alert area, only the pilots training there must watch for other traffic.
cards.why: No. Pilots training there and pilots passing through are equally responsible for collision avoidance [[33:191|AIM 3-4-6]].

cards.s: Every TFR is drawn on the sectional chart.
cards.why: No. Only TFRs related to national security are charted. Check the NOTAMs for the rest [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

cards.s: A controlled firing area means you must change your route.
cards.why: No. The firing stops when an aircraft comes near, so you do not need to change your path [[33:191|AIM 3-4-7]].

cards.s: You may fly through a VFR corridor in Class B without a clearance.
cards.why: Yes. A corridor is a "hole" through Class B. No clearance or ATC contact is needed [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].

cards.s: A warning area starts 3 NM out from the U.S. coast.
cards.why: Yes. Warning areas extend from 3 NM outward from the coast and warn of hazardous activity [[33:191|AIM 3-4-4]].

activities.title: Read the airspace legend
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Box with the Class C approach frequency to call
Class D from the surface up to but not including 2,700 ft MSL
Class E that begins at the surface (dashed magenta)
Class E floor 700 ft AGL next to Class G (magenta vignette)
Class E floor 1,200 ft AGL next to Class G (blue vignette)

final_quiz.q: Which of these is nonregulatory special use airspace?
options: A military operations area (MOA)
A restricted area
A prohibited area
Class D airspace
final_quiz.why: MOAs, warning, alert, controlled firing and national security areas are nonregulatory. Prohibited and restricted areas and Classes A to E are regulatory [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a fast airplane beneath a Class B shelf, outside Class B. What is the highest indicated airspeed allowed?
options: 250 knots
150 knots
230 knots
200 knots
final_quiz.why: Under a Class B shelf or in a VFR corridor, the limit is 200 knots (230 mph). The 250-knot limit is for the rest of the airspace below 10,000 MSL [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a),(c)]].

final_quiz.q: Calling a Class D tower, you hear: "Cessna 5KM, remain outside the Class Delta and standby." What do you do?
options: Enter, since they used your call sign to reply
Stay outside until the tower says you may enter
Enter, but stay above the pattern altitude
Squawk 7600 and enter, since the tower is busy
final_quiz.why: "Remain outside" means ATC cannot take you yet, even though it used your call sign. Hold outside the Class D until told otherwise [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

final_quiz.q: By day you cruise at exactly 1,200 feet AGL. Class E starts at 1,200 feet AGL here. Which VFR minimums apply?
options: 3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
1 SM and clear of clouds
5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
1 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
final_quiz.why: At the base altitude of Class E you count as being in the airspace below it, which is Class G at 1,200 AGL or less: 1 SM and clear of clouds by day [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]] [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You cruise at 10,500 feet MSL over a high plateau. The ground below you is 8,500 feet MSL. You are far from any Class B or Class C airspace and from every airport listed in Part 91 Appendix D. Do you need an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out?
options: Yes, both are always required at or above 10,000 feet MSL
Yes, because the ground below you is high
No, because you are within 2,500 feet of the surface
Only at night
final_quiz.why: The transponder and ADS-B Out rules for at and above 10,000 feet MSL both exclude the airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL. You are only 2,000 feet above the ground (10,500 - 8,500) [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: At night you fly the traffic pattern at a Class G airport, 700 feet AGL and within 1/2 mile of the runway. Flight visibility is 2 SM. What is the rule?
options: You may fly clear of clouds
You need 3 SM, so you must leave the pattern
You need a special VFR clearance
You must stay 500 feet below the clouds
final_quiz.why: In Class G below 1,200 AGL at night, an airplane in the pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway may fly clear of clouds with at least 1 SM visibility [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: It is daytime. Your Class D airport reports visibility 6 SM and an overcast ceiling at 800 feet. You are a private pilot with no instrument rating. What can you do to depart?
options: Depart VFR, since visibility is over 3 SM and it reports VFR
Ask ATC for special VFR; if cleared, stay clear of clouds
Nothing, special VFR is only for instrument-rated pilots
Depart VFR if you stay 500 feet below the clouds
final_quiz.why: No VFR beneath a ceiling under 1,000 feet in a surface area, except special VFR [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. By day, a non-instrument pilot can get SVFR: clearance, clear of clouds, 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

final_quiz.q: A student pilot on a day solo flies in Class G at 1,000 feet AGL. Flight visibility drops to 2 SM. What is true?
options: Not legal, because a student needs at least 3 SM by day
Legal, because Class G needs only 1 SM
Legal if the student stays clear of clouds
Not legal, because a student needs at least 5 SM by day
final_quiz.why: Students may not act as PIC with flight or surface visibility under 3 SM by day (5 SM at night), even where 91.155 allows less [[60:278|14 CFR 61.89(a)(6)]].

final_quiz.q: A Class D ceiling on the chart is shown in a box as -30. What does it mean?
options: Floor of 3,000 feet MSL, not the ceiling
Ceiling of 3,000 feet AGL, from the airport surface
Ceiling of 300 feet MSL, read straight from the box
Surface up to but not including 3,000 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: A minus in front of the Class D ceiling means from the surface to, but not including, that altitude. Charted altitudes drop the last two zeros and are MSL [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

final_quiz.q: Your route crosses a military training route labeled VR1257. What does the four-digit number tell you?
options: Jets there are limited to 250 knots by the number
Some segments are above 1,500 feet AGL
The route is used only under IFR, so no VFR traffic
The route has no segment above 1,500 feet AGL
final_quiz.why: Four digits mean no segment above 1,500 feet AGL; three digits mean at least one segment is higher. MTR traffic is often faster than 250 knots [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2]] [[33:193|AIM 3-5-2]].

final_quiz.q: A TFR is issued for aircraft fighting a forest fire. If the NOTAM is a typical one, what airspace does it cover?
options: Up to 1,000 feet AGL within 1 NM
Up to 10,000 feet MSL within 10 NM
Up to 2,000 feet above the surface within 3 NM
Up to 18,000 feet MSL within 30 NM
final_quiz.why: Disaster and relief TFRs are normally within 2,000 feet above the surface and a 3 NM radius. Always read the actual NOTAM, since sizes vary [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a VFR flight to an airport 45 NM from the DCA VOR/DME, outside the DC SFRA. What extra step does the FAA require?
options: File an IFR flight plan
Complete the FAA Special Awareness Training
Hold an instrument rating
Nothing, since you stay outside the SFRA
final_quiz.why: A pilot flying VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME must complete Special Awareness Training, not just pilots who enter the SFRA [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Inside Class C, approach gives you a heading that will take you into a cloud ahead. What should you do?
options: Fly the heading, since ATC is responsible for weather
Tell approach and get a revised instruction
Turn away without saying anything
Climb above the cloud on your own
final_quiz.why: ATC service does not relieve you of VFR weather minimums. Advise approach and get a revised clearance or instruction [[33:184|AIM 3-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: A magenta dashed line surrounds an airport. What does it mark?
options: Class E airspace that starts at the surface
Class D airspace around a towered airport
Class C airspace around a busy airport
A Terminal Radar Service Area around the airport
final_quiz.why: Class E surface airspace is symbolized by a magenta dashed line. Class D is a blue dashed line [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]] [[2:27|Chart Users' Guide p 27]].

final_quiz.q: The legend says an ADIZ is an area where what is required?
options: Radio silence for every aircraft in it
Ready identification, location and control of aircraft
Military training flights only, no civil flights
Weather minimums are lowered for all aircraft flying in it
final_quiz.why: An ADIZ is an area in which the ready identification, location and control of all aircraft is required in the interest of national security [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

final_quiz.q: A restricted area on your route is active. Under 14 CFR 91.133(a), when may you operate in it?
options: Any time your transponder is on and reporting
Any time you are above 3,000 ft AGL
Any time you are on a flight following service
Only with permission of the using or controlling agency
final_quiz.why: No person may operate an aircraft within a restricted area contrary to its restrictions unless that person has the permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].
